en: The Hymn to the Sacred Tradition (Āmnāya)
In order to establish his renown in the four famous directions,
the Lord established four monasteries after his own name and installed his disciples there.
The Teacher assigned distinct names to these four according to their different titles.
He indeed ordained the field, the deity, the power, and the sacred ford individually;
likewise, he established the tradition and the various branches of the Vedic scriptures for the celibate students,
all for the benefit of the world.
In the western quarter lies the sacred field of Dvārakā and the Śāradāmaṭha;
there are the Kīṭavāla tradition and both the Tīrtha and Āśrama sites.
The deity is Siddheśvara, and the Śakti is renowned as Bhadrakālī.
The preceptor known as Svarūpabrahmacārī is Padmapādaka;
he will be the renowned Gomatī-tīrtha, and the Sāmaveda will reside therein,
where the realization of the unity of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) shall arise.
That famous great statement, "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), is the [central] utterance.
In the eastern direction, the Govardhana Maṭha is remembered as the second;
the Bhogavalla Sampradāya is established in the Sattrāraṇya forest.
In that place dwells the Lord of the World, known by the name Puruṣottama;
the field is the goddess Vṛṣalā, renowned throughout all the worlds;
and the manifest Brahmachārī is known by the name Hastāmalaka.
The preceptor there is renowned in the worlds by that name;
the great ocean is declared to be the sacred bathing place (tīrtha), and the Ṛgveda is proclaimed [as the mantra]. And the Great Statement (mahāvākya) spoken there is "Prajñānam Brahma."
In the north shall be the Śrī Maṭha; the sacred field is Badarikāśrama.
The deity is named Nārāyaṇa, and the Śakti is Pūrṇagiri. The Sampradāya is Ānandavana, and the Tīrtha is Ālakanandikā.
Ānanda, Brahmachārī, Giri, Parvata, and Sāgara are the names; Totakācārya is known as Vedodharvaṇa.
And therein, this Great Saying (Mahāvākya) is proclaimed: "This Self is Brahman."
The fourth is the Śāradā Maṭha in Śṛṅgerī to the south;
there stands the Liṅga that destroys impurity, which was well-worshipped by Vibhāṇḍaka,
and where lies the great hermitage of the great seer Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
The deity there is Varāha, and that place is proclaimed as Rāmakṣetra;
the sacred ford is named Tuṅgabhadrā, and the Śakti is known as Śrīśāradā.
The preceptor there is renowned as Caitanyabrahmacārī.
The author of the Vārttika and other works on the knowledge of Brahman, who is honored by sages,
is Sureśvarācārya, an actual incarnation of Brahmā.
Sarasvatīpurī and Bhāratyāraṇyatīrtha are [his] two sacred sites.
The names beginning with "Giri" (Mountain) and "Āśrama" (Hermitage) are always used as common nouns.
The Yajurveda is declared to have many branches and a vast tradition.
Therein, the Great Saying (Mahāvākya) is proclaimed: "I am Brahman."
The names of the four deities, their powers, and the sacred fields are given in sequence;
likewise, the great sayings and the Vedas have all been declared according to their systematic arrangement.
Thus [ends the work] of the illustrious king of wandering mendicants (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka).
By reciting the *Āmnāyastotra* and other such hymns, one attains a virtuous state both in this world and the next;
at the end of the body, one attains liberation—of this there is no doubt. (22) Thus ends the *Āmnāyastotra*.
